PC1-franklin-chart-01.kicker: One Book, One Idea, One Action
PC1-franklin-chart-01.claim: Benjamin Franklin kept a chart of his own faults.
PC1-franklin-chart-01.sub: It didn’t go well. That was the point.

PC1-franklin-chart-02.term: A young printer with a plan
PC1-franklin-chart-02.definition: Franklin decided to work on his character on purpose, one trait at a time, and to keep score.

PC1-franklin-chart-03.definition: Temperance, Silence, Order, Resolution, Frugality, Industry, Sincerity, Justice, Moderation, Cleanliness, Tranquillity, Chastity, Humility.
PC1-franklin-chart-03.cite: Franklin, Autobiography ch. IX · Standard Ebooks

PC1-franklin-chart-04.definition: A little book, a page per virtue, a column per day. One virtue got his full attention each week, so all thirteen fitted in thirteen weeks.

PC1-franklin-chart-05.quote: I was surprised to find myself so much fuller of faults than I had imagined; but I had the satisfaction of seeing them diminish.
PC1-franklin-chart-05.note: Franklin, on his first pages of dots.
PC1-franklin-chart-05.cite: Franklin, Autobiography ch. IX · Standard Ebooks

PC1-franklin-chart-06.definition: “My scheme of Order gave me the most trouble.” He admits it never quite stuck. He kept the book anyway.
PC1-franklin-chart-06.cite: Franklin, Autobiography ch. IX · Standard Ebooks

PC1-franklin-chart-07.title: One trait. One week.
PC1-franklin-chart-07.body: One dot per slip. Count on Sunday. The goal isn’t a clean page. It’s noticing.

PC1-franklin-chart-08.line: Watching a habit is the first thing that changes it.
PC1-franklin-chart-08.action: Researched introduction: no personal review yet. The Autobiography is free to read. Which virtue first?

PC2-thank-you-note-01.claim: You think a thank-you note would be awkward.

PC2-thank-you-note-02.definition: Psychologists asked people to write a short note of gratitude to someone who had mattered to them, then guess how it would land.

PC2-thank-you-note-03.definition: Writers expected the recipient to feel more awkward, and less surprised and happy, than the recipients reported feeling.

PC2-thank-you-note-04.definition: Writers worried about getting the words right. Recipients cared about the warmth. (Moodius’s reading of the study.)

PC2-thank-you-note-05.title: Three lines. One person. Today.
PC2-thank-you-note-05.body: What they did. What it changed. That you’re grateful. Send it before you edit it.

PC2-thank-you-note-06.line: The thank-you you keep not sending is probably welcome.
PC2-thank-you-note-06.action: Send this to the friend you’ve been meaning to thank. Who’s owed one?

PC3-metta-01.claim: A 2,500-year-old practice for the person who annoys you.

PC3-metta-02.definition: A short Buddhist text on goodwill. It covers everyone: seen and unseen, near and far, and the people you would rather skip.
PC3-metta-02.cite: Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata I.8 · tr. V. Fausböll, 1881

PC3-metta-03.quote: As a mother at the risk of her life watches over her own child, her only child, so also let every one cultivate a boundless (friendly) mind towards all beings.
PC3-metta-03.cite: Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata I.8 · tr. V. Fausböll, 1881

PC3-metta-04.quote: Let no one deceive another, let him not despise (another) in any place, … let him not out of anger or resentment wish harm to another.
PC3-metta-04.cite: Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata I.8 · tr. V. Fausböll, 1881

PC3-metta-05.definition: Not liking them. Not agreeing. A short private wish that they go well. It’s called a practice because you repeat it, badly, until it’s less bad.

PC3-metta-06.definition: A 2015 review of 24 studies (1,759 people) found medium gains in daily positive mood. Many studies were small or at risk of bias. Linked, not proven.
PC3-metta-06.cite: Zeng et al., Frontiers in Psychology, 2015

PC3-metta-07.line: Pick one person. Thirty seconds. Nobody has to know.
PC3-metta-07.action: Send this to the friend who’s still annoyed about last week. Who’s yours?

PC4-onesimus-01.claim: In 1721 Boston, an enslaved man explained how to stop smallpox.

PC4-onesimus-02.definition: A West African man enslaved by the minister Cotton Mather. He described a procedure from home: a little matter from a smallpox sore, scratched into the skin, and the person was protected.
PC4-onesimus-02.cite: Mather, letter to the Royal Society, 1716

PC4-onesimus-03.definition: Smallpox hit Boston. The doctor Zabdiel Boylston tried the method Onesimus had described. Most of the town’s doctors and press were furious.

PC4-onesimus-04.definition: Of roughly 280 people inoculated, about six died. Of the thousands who caught smallpox the usual way, about one in seven did.

PC4-onesimus-05.tag: The part that gets left out
PC4-onesimus-05.definition: The method was common in West Africa and in Asia long before Boston. Onesimus tried to buy his freedom in 1716. History books named the minister.

PC4-onesimus-06.line: The expert in the room isn’t always the one being asked.
PC4-onesimus-06.action: History, not medical advice: inoculation of this kind was risky and is no longer used. Would you have listened?

PS1-granua-fact.label: Sunday fact
lines: Marcus Aurelius wrote Book 1 of the Meditations in an army camp.
The last line of the book says where: “Among the Quadi at the Granua”, a frontier war on the Danube.
No audience. No performance. That’s why it still reads like a real person.
PS1-granua-fact.footer: The diary carousel is on the grid at 12:00

PS2-journal-enough.label: Sunday journal
lines: Money, work, people, rest. Pick one and describe the day you’d stop pushing.
Add your answer below if you like. Nobody else sees it.
